refibra.types: REFIBRA is not sold as a fiber on its own; it is a technology tag applied to other Lenzing fibers. The two product families are TENCEL Lyocell with REFIBRA technology, where Lenzing now describes recycled cotton pulp content of 30% or more, and LENZING ECOVERO viscose made with REFIBRA technology. The recycled share has risen since the 2017 launch (from about 20%) and the input mix has shifted from pre-consumer cutting scraps toward including post-consumer cotton garments. There are no separate grades by strength or denier beyond those of the host fiber, so a buyer specifies the lyocell or viscose type first and the REFIBRA content second.
refibra.fabrics: REFIBRA lyocell appears in the same places as TENCEL lyocell: denim, shirting, knit tops, bedding and towels, often in blends with cotton or recycled cotton. REFIBRA viscose is used in fluid dress fabrics, jersey and printed wovens. Because the recycled content is inside the fiber and the finished fabric is often blended, a garment that says 'made with REFIBRA' may contain a modest overall recycled share. Brands have used it mainly in capsule collections and denim lines that advertise circular content.
refibra.quality: Check that the label gives the generic fiber (lyocell or viscose) and, if a recycled claim is made, a percentage for the whole product. Ask the brand what share of the lyocell or viscose is recycled pulp and what share of the garment that fiber represents; a garment of 30% REFIBRA lyocell with 30% recycled pulp contains only about 9% recycled cotton. Documentation such as transaction certificates under a recycled-content standard and Lenzing's fiber identification can support the claim. Fabric quality is judged exactly as for lyocell or viscose: even surface, low pilling, clean seams.
pros: It returns cotton cutting scraps and some post-consumer cotton to fiber production instead of landfill or incineration.
The finished fiber behaves like standard lyocell or viscose, so mills can use it without changing processes.
It reduces the wood pulp needed per tonne of fiber by the recycled share.
Lenzing's fiber identification allows branded content to be checked in finished goods.
cons: Most of the fiber is still wood pulp, so 'recycled' claims can overstate the circular share.
Recycled share is diluted again when the fiber is blended with other materials in the garment.
Cotton waste with polyester, elastane or heavy finishes is hard to use, which limits the feedstock.
Recycled content cannot be detected chemically; buyers rely on documentation.
refibra.impact: Lenzing presents REFIBRA as reducing virgin wood demand and diverting cotton waste, which follows logically from replacing part of the pulp; the size of any net benefit depends on the energy and chemicals used to purify colored, finished cotton waste, which Lenzing reports in its own life-cycle data. No independent peer-reviewed life-cycle study specific to REFIBRA was found for this entry. General evidence for regenerated cellulose applies: a 2019 NC State study found rayon microfibers biodegraded in aerobic aquatic tests while polyester microfibers persisted. Recycled-content claims in the US fall under the FTC Green Guides (16 CFR Part 260), which expect claims to be qualified and substantiated. Chain-of-custody standards such as Textile Exchange's Content Claim Standard exist to carry such claims through the supply chain.
refibra.care: Care follows the host fiber. For REFIBRA lyocell: wash at 30 to 40 C on a gentle cycle, inside out, with mild detergent, avoid overloading to limit fibrillation, and iron at medium heat (about 150 C) while slightly damp. For REFIBRA viscose: wash cold to 30 C, do not wring, dry flat or hanging, and iron on medium on the reverse. Both are cellulose, so avoid chlorine bleach and store dry to prevent mildew. Recycled content does not change care needs. Where the garment is a blend with elastane or polyester, the most heat-sensitive component and the label set the limits.
faq: No. It is Lenzing's name for a technology that puts recycled cotton pulp into its lyocell and viscose fibers. The garment label still has to name the fiber, such as lyocell or viscose, and any recycled claim should state a percentage.
How much recycled content does REFIBRA contain?

Lenzing started at about 20% recycled cotton pulp in 2017 and now describes 30% or more for TENCEL lyocell with REFIBRA, the rest being wood pulp. The share in a finished garment is lower if the fiber is blended with other materials.
Can REFIBRA garments be recycled again?

In principle, cellulose fiber can be pulped again, and the same route that uses cotton waste could use lyocell waste. In practice, blends with polyester or elastane, dyes and finishes make recycling harder, and collection systems for post-consumer textiles are still limited.
notable: A garment with 30% REFIBRA lyocell whose fiber holds 30% recycled pulp contains only about 9% recycled cotton overall.
REFIBRA started with pre-consumer cotton scraps from garment cutting rooms and later added post-consumer cotton textiles.
